title: A Blanket of Light
caption: The Blanco 4-meter Telescope under green airglow and the Milky Way, Cerro Tololo
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile stands against the bright Milky Way. Above a layer of clouds, the sky glows green.

That green light is airglow. It appears when trace particles and gases in the atmosphere become electrically charged, or ionized. At night their atoms recombine and give off light of their own, producing a faint glow across the sky.

Airglow is so faint that people seldom see it with the naked eye. Long-exposure photographs like this one capture it more easily. It is one reason the night sky is never completely dark, even at sites far from light pollution. On its own, though, it does not usually cause serious trouble for astronomers observing at night.
